Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 56, verses 1–6:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾. He, exalted is He, means by His words ﴿When the Event occurs﴾: when the Blast of the Resurrection descends, which is when the Trumpet is blown for the establishment of the Hour.

As related:

* I was told on the authority of al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words ﴿When the Event occurs﴾, that it means: the Blast.

* 'Ali narrated to us, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, on the authority of 'Ali, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿When the Event occurs﴾: "The Event," "the Overwhelming," and "the Deafening," and similar names of the Resurrection, which Allah has magnified and by which He has warned His servants.

* * *

And His words: ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾.

He, exalted is He, says: There is no denial of the occurrence of the Event, nor any repelling or reversal of it. Here al-kadhiba (denial) is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-'aqiba (outcome) and al-'afiya (well-being).

Those versed in interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said.

Who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazid narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, on the authority of Qatada, concerning ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾: that is, there is no reversal of it, no return, and no turning back.

* Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Qatada, concerning His words ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾, and he said: "No reversal."

* * *

And His words: ﴿Abasing and exalting﴾.

He, exalted is He, says: The Event at that time abases a people who were honoured in this world, sending them down to the Fire of Allah.

* * *

And His words: ﴿exalting﴾.

He says: It exalts a people who were humbled in this world, raising them to the mercy of Allah and His Garden. It has also been said: it abases, so that it makes the nearest hear, and it exalts, so that it makes the farthest hear.

Who said what we have said:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, who said: 'Ubayd Allah, meaning al-'Ataki, narrated to us, on the authority of 'Uthman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Suraqa, concerning ﴿abasing and exalting﴾: The Hour abases the enemies of Allah to the Fire and exalts the friends of Allah to the Garden.

* Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazid narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, on the authority of Qatada, concerning His words ﴿abasing and exalting﴾, who said: It penetrates every plain and mountain until it makes the near and the far hear; then it exalts a people in the honour of Allah and abases a people in the punishment of Allah.

* Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Qatada, ﴿abasing and exalting﴾, and he said: It makes the near and the far hear, abasing a people to the punishment of Allah and exalting a people to the honour of Allah.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, who said: al-Husayn narrated to us, on the authority of Yazid, on the authority of 'Ikrima, concerning His words ﴿abasing and exalting﴾, who said: It abases and makes the nearest hear, and exalts and makes the farthest hear; he said: So the near and the far were equal before Allah.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, who said: My father narrated to me, who said: My paternal uncle narrated to me, who said: My father narrated to me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿abasing and exalting﴾, he said: It made the near and the far hear.

* I was told on the authority of al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words ﴿abasing and exalting﴾: It abased and made the nearest hear, and it exalted and made the farthest hear, so that the near and the far were equal in it.

* * *

And His words: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾.

He, exalted is He, says: When the earth is shaken and violently agitated, from the saying "the arrow vibrates in the target" (yartajju fi al-gharad), meaning: it trembles and quakes.

Those versed in interpretation have said something similar to what we have said.

Who said that:

* 'Ali narrated to me, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, on the authority of 'Ali, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾: he said: He shook it.

* Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, who said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, who said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, who said: al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Warqa' narrated to us, all on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, the saying of Allah ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾: he said: It was shaken with an earthquake.

* Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazid narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, on the authority of Qatada, concerning His words ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾: he said: It was shaken with a quake.

* Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Qatada, ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾, he said: It was shaken with a violent quaking.

* * *

And His words: ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾.

He, exalted is He, says: The mountains are broken into fragments, becoming like flour that has been moistened (al-mabsus), which is the moistened one, just as He, may His praise be glorified, said: ﴿and the mountains will become heaps of loose sand﴾. Al-basisa among the Arabs is flour or roasted meal, which is kneaded and made into provisions.

It is related of a highwayman from Ghatafan that he wanted to bake bread, but feared he would be hurried before baking and would eat it as dough, and he said:

"Do not bake bread, do not crush and bake, (but) drive the she-camels swiftly, swiftly, away from the pasture of al-Halasi, swiftly."[[This verse is one of the examples cited by Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 174b) at the words of the Exalted ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾. He said: Its figurative sense is like the figurative sense of moistened roasted meal, that is, moistened and kneaded. A highwayman from Ghatafan said, when he wanted to bake bread and feared he would be hurried before baking the flour, so he ate it as dough, and he said: "Do not bake bread, do not crush and bake." End. In (al-Lisan: m-l-s): al-Mals: a strong driving. In b-s: Tha'lab said: the meaning of "the mountains are crushed to powder" is: they were mixed with dust. Some said: they were pulverised; some said: they were levelled. End. Abu 'Ubayda did not cite the second verse; the author of al-Lisan cited the first verse and followed it with another verse, which is: "Nor prolong (the journey) at the resting place of Hays." He cited the second verse under "m-l-s", and said: al-Mals: a strong driving. It is said: "malastu bil-ibil amlusu" (from the pattern qatala) "malsan," when you drive the camels stealthily. The rajiz said: "Swiftly, driving away the Halasi." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-Mals is a kind of fine travel, and al-Mals is softness of anything. End. Al-Farra' cited the two verses in Ma'ani al-Qur'an as in the author's version. He said (folio 322): "and the mountains are crushed to powder": they became like flour, and this is His words "and the mountains will be set in motion." I heard the Arabs recite: "Do not bake bread..." the two verses. Al-Basisa among them is flour or roasted meal, which is kneaded and made into provisions. End. In al-Nawadir of Abu Zayd (Beirut, p. 11): "Driving swiftly, away from the Humasi, swiftly ... from a day's grazing until the sun seems ... at the western horizon, dyed with saffron." Abu Zayd said: al-Mals: a fierce march. Abu Hatim said: I say, not on Abu Zayd's authority: al-Mals is a quick, easy march. His words "dyed with saffron" mean: it has turned yellow at sunset. End.]] And those versed in interpretation have said something similar to what we have said.

Who said that:

* 'Ali narrated to me, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, on the authority of 'Ali, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: They were pulverised into powder.

* al-Harith narrated to me, who said: al-Hasan narrated to us, who said: Warqa' narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: They were broken to pieces.

* Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, who said: Sufyan narrated to us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: Like the drying of roasted meal.

* Ahmad ibn 'Amr al-Basri narrated to me, who said: Hafs ibn 'Umar al-'Adani narrated to us, on the authority of al-Hakam ibn Aban, on the authority of 'Ikrima, ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: They were pulverised into powder.

* Isma'il ibn Musa, the son of the daughter of al-Suddi, narrated to me, who said: Bishr ibn al-Hakam al-Ahmasi informed us, on the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Salt, on the authority of Isma'il al-Suddi and Abu Salih, concerning ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: They were ground to powder.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Mihran narrated to us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: Like the drying of roasted meal.

* Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, concerning the words of Allah ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: they became a heap of loose sand, as Allah said.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Jarir narrated to us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿and the mountains are crushed to powder﴾: he said: They were pulverised into powder.

* * *

And His words: ﴿so they become scattered dust motes﴾.

The people of interpretation differed about the meaning of al-hiba' (scattered dust). Some said: it is the ray of the sun which enters through a window, like dust.

Who said that:

* 'Ali narrated to me, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, on the authority of 'Ali, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿so they become scattered dust motes﴾: he said: the rays of the sun.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Hakam narrated to us, on the authority of 'Amr, on the authority of 'Ata', on the authority of Sa'id, ﴿scattered dust motes﴾: he said: the ray of the sun when it enters through a window.

* He said: Jarir narrated to us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿so they become scattered dust motes﴾: he said: the ray of the sun entering through a window, and it is nothing.

Others said: it is the dust raised by beasts.

Who said that:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Mihran narrated to us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, on the authority of al-Harith, on the authority of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the dust of the beasts.

Others said: it is what flies off as sparks of fire, which has no substance.

Who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, who said: My father narrated to me, who said: My paternal uncle narrated to me, who said: My father narrated to me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿so they become scattered dust motes﴾: he said: The hiba' is what flies off from fire when it blazes; sparks fly from it, and when they fall they are nothing.

Others said: it is the dried-up foliage of trees which the winds scatter.

Who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazid narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, on the authority of Qatada, concerning His words ﴿so they become scattered dust motes﴾: like the dried foliage of trees, scattered by the winds to the right and to the left.

* Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Qatada, concerning His words ﴿scattered dust motes﴾: he said: The hiba' is the debris of trees which the wind scatters.

We have already explained the meaning of hiba' in another place with its evidence, so there is no need to repeat it here.

As for His words ﴿scattered﴾, it means: dispersed.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 56, verses 7–12:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will be three kinds (azwājan thalāthah)﴾ [56:7] to ﴿in gardens of bliss﴾ [56:12].

Almighty God says: And you, O people, will be kinds (anwā'an) three and types (ḍurūban).

As related:

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾, he said: "The ranks of the people on the Day of Resurrection."

* *

And His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right—what are the companions of the right!﴾

This is an explanation from God concerning the three kinds. He, may His praise be exalted, says: "And you will be three kinds: the companions of the right, the companions of the left, and the foremost." He made the report about them sufficient in place of explaining them in the manner we have mentioned, since the speech indicates its meaning. So He said: ﴿So the companions of the right—what are the companions of the right!﴾, amazing His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) about them. And He said: ﴿The companions of the right﴾, those by whom one is taken on the right side to Paradise—what a thing are the companions of the right! ﴿And the companions of the left—what are the companions of the left!﴾ Almighty God says: And the companions of the left are those by whom one is taken on the left side to the Fire. And His saying: ﴿In gardens of bliss﴾

He says: in gardens of enduring bliss.

Concerning the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples, and a few from the later ones, reclining on jeweled thrones, facing one another, reclining upon them. Youths of everlasting youth will circulate among them with cups, pitchers, and a glass from a flowing spring, by which they will not be harmed nor made drunk, and with fruit of their choosing, and the flesh of birds that they desire.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: a multitude of the past nations, and a few of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ. They are "the later ones" (*al-akhirun*), and it was said they were called "the later ones" because they are the last of the nations. ﴿On thrones woven together﴾ means: upon thrones woven and interlaced, with some parts inserted into others, just as the rings of a coat of mail are interlocked one over another in a double layer. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"And of the weaving of Dawud, a woven (mawdunah) [seat], carried along with the tribe, camel-load after camel-load."* [[This verse is from A'sha of Banu Qays ibn Tha'labah (his Diwan, Cairo edition, p. 99), from a qasidah in praise of Hawdhah ibn Ali al-Hanafi. Before the verse is: "And you prepared for war its gear... long spears and male horses." "Awzar al-harb" means its equipment; "dir' mawdunah" is a coat of mail woven closely, one part over another; "tusaq ma'a al-hayy" means carried along. He says: you prepared for war its equipment: long spears, noble horses, and thick coats of mail woven in a double weave, carried on camels, one caravan after another. Abu Ubaydah said in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 174b), at the phrase "on thrones woven together": one part over another, interlaced, as the rings of a coat of mail are interlocked in a double layer. And al-A'sha said: "And of the weaving of Dawud..." The *wadin* is the strap of a saddle-girth when it is woven one part over another in double layers like the rings of mail; it is called *wadin*, and *mawdun* is used in the place of *mawdun*, as they say *qatil* in the place of *maqtul*. He said: "To you it runs anxiously, its girth..."]]

From it comes the *wadin* of the she-camel, which is the girth of woven straps, woven one part over another in double layers like the rings of a coat of mail. It was also said: *wadin*, but it is actually *mawdun*, changed from the passive participle to the form *fa'il*, as one says *qatil* for *maqtul*. It was transmitted by hearing from some Arabs: "the bricks of the kiln are *mawdun*, one laid over another," meaning stacked and arranged in rows.

It was also said: they are called "woven thrones" only because they are interlaced with gold and gems.

Mention of those who said this:

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Husayn narrated to us, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿on thrones woven together﴾, he said: "adorned with gold."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Husayn, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿on thrones woven together﴾, he said: "adorned with gold."

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿on thrones woven together﴾, he said: it means beds adorned (*al-asirrah al-murmalah*).

• Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Husayn, from Mujahid, who said: "*al-mawdunah*: adorned with gold."

"Awzar al-harb" means its equipment; "dir' mawdunah" is a coat of mail woven closely, one part over another; "tusaq ma'a al-hayy" means carried along. He says: you prepared for war its equipment: long spears, noble horses, and thick coats of mail woven in a double weave, carried on camels, one caravan after another. And al-A'sha said: "And of the weaving of Dawud..." The *wadin* is the strap of a saddle-girth when it is woven one part over another in double layers like the rings of mail; it is called *wadin*, and *mawdun* is used in the place of *mawdun*, as they say *qatil* in the place of *maqtul*. And His words: ﴿nor made drunk﴾

The readers (*qurra'*) differed in its recitation. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿yunzafun﴾ with a fathah on the *zay*, and they understood it to mean that their minds are not impaired. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿la yunzifun﴾ with a kasrah on the *zay*, in the sense: and their drink will not run out.

In my view, the correct position is that both are well-known recitations (*qira'atan*) with sound meanings, so whichever one the reader recites is correct.

The people of ta'wil differed in the interpretation of this, in line with the difference among the readers. And His words: ﴿and fruit of their choosing﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: these everlasting youths will circulate among these foremost ones with fruit from the fruits of Paradise that they choose for themselves, which their souls desire, ﴿and the flesh of birds that they desire﴾. He says: they will also circulate among them with the flesh of birds, of whatever birds their souls desire.

Concerning the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples, and a few from the later ones, reclining on jeweled thrones, facing one another, reclining upon them. Youths of everlasting youth will circulate among them with cups, pitchers, and a glass from a flowing spring, by which they will not be harmed nor made drunk, and with fruit of their choosing, and the flesh of birds that they desire.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: a multitude of the past nations, and a few of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ. They are "the later ones" (*al-akhirun*), and it was said they were called "the later ones" because they are the last of the nations. ﴿On thrones woven together﴾ means: upon thrones woven and interlaced, with some parts inserted into others, just as the rings of a coat of mail are interlocked one over another in a double layer. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"And of the weaving of Dawud, a woven (mawdunah) [seat], carried along with the tribe, camel-load after camel-load."* [[This verse is from A'sha of Banu Qays ibn Tha'labah (his Diwan, Cairo edition, p. 99), from a qasidah in praise of Hawdhah ibn Ali al-Hanafi. Before the verse is: "And you prepared for war its gear... long spears and male horses." "Awzar al-harb" means its equipment; "dir' mawdunah" is a coat of mail woven closely, one part over another; "tusaq ma'a al-hayy" means carried along. He says: you prepared for war its equipment: long spears, noble horses, and thick coats of mail woven in a double weave, carried on camels, one caravan after another. Abu Ubaydah said in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 174b), at the phrase "on thrones woven together": one part over another, interlaced, as the rings of a coat of mail are interlocked in a double layer. And al-A'sha said: "And of the weaving of Dawud..." The *wadin* is the strap of a saddle-girth when it is woven one part over another in double layers like the rings of mail; it is called *wadin*, and *mawdun* is used in the place of *mawdun*, as they say *qatil* in the place of *maqtul*. He said: "To you it runs anxiously, its girth..."]]

From it comes the *wadin* of the she-camel, which is the girth of woven straps, woven one part over another in double layers like the rings of a coat of mail. It was also said: *wadin*, but it is actually *mawdun*, changed from the passive participle to the form *fa'il*, as one says *qatil* for *maqtul*. It was transmitted by hearing from some Arabs: "the bricks of the kiln are *mawdun*, one laid over another," meaning stacked and arranged in rows.

It was also said: they are called "woven thrones" only because they are interlaced with gold and gems.

• Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Husayn, from Mujahid, who said: "*al-mawdunah*: adorned with gold."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Waqid narrated to us, from Yazid, from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿on thrones woven together﴾, he said: "interlaced with pearls and rubies."

• Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿woven﴾, he said: "adorned with gold."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿on thrones woven together﴾: "*al-mawdunah* is the *al-marmulah*, which is the best of thrones."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, regarding His words ﴿woven﴾, he said: "*marmulah*."

• Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, regarding His words ﴿on thrones woven together﴾, he said: "*marmulah*, interlaced."

• It was reported to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿on thrones woven together﴾: "*al-wadn* is the interlacing and weaving; he means the middle part is interlaced and woven."

And His words: ﴿nor made drunk﴾

The readers (*qurra'*) differed in its recitation. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿yunzafun﴾ with a fathah on the *zay*, and they understood it to mean that their minds are not impaired. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿la yunzifun﴾ with a kasrah on the *zay*, in the sense: and their drink will not run out.

In my view, the correct position is that both are well-known recitations (*qira'atan*) with sound meanings, so whichever one the reader recites is correct.

The people of ta'wil differed in the interpretation of this, in line with the difference among the readers. We have mentioned the range of their opinions and clarified the correct position in Surat al-Saffat, so that suffices here; nonetheless, we will mention the view of some of them here, lest someone think its meaning here differs from its meaning there.

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿by which they will not be harmed﴾: "It has no headache."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿by which they will not be harmed﴾, he said: "their heads will not be split."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿by which they will not be harmed﴾, he says: "their heads will not be split."

• It was reported to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿by which they will not be harmed﴾: he means "headache."

* *

And His words: ﴿nor made drunk﴾

The readers (*qurra'*) differed in its recitation. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿yunzafun﴾ with a fathah on the *zay*, and they understood it to mean that their minds are not impaired. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿la yunzifun﴾ with a kasrah on the *zay*, in the sense: and their drink will not run out.

In my view, the correct position is that both are well-known recitations (*qira'atan*) with sound meanings, so whichever one the reader recites is correct.

The people of ta'wil differed in the interpretation of this, in line with the difference among the readers. We have mentioned the range of their opinions and clarified the correct position in Surat al-Saffat, so that suffices here; nonetheless, we will mention the view of some of them here, lest someone think its meaning here differs from its meaning there.

Mention of those who said: its meaning is that their minds will not be impaired:

• Isma'il ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Shurayk informed us, from Salim, from Sa'id, regarding ﴿nor made drunk﴾, he said: "their minds will not be impaired."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿nor made drunk﴾, he said: "their minds will not be impaired."

• And Ibn Humayd narrated to us again, and said: "their minds will not be lost."

• It was reported to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding ﴿nor made drunk﴾: "their minds will not be impaired."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding (nor made drunk), he said: "No one will be overcome in his mind."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, regarding ﴿nor made drunk﴾, he said: "No one will be overcome in his mind."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding God's words ﴿nor made drunk﴾, he said: "their minds will not be overcome."

* *

And His words: ﴿and fruit of their choosing﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: these everlasting youths will circulate among these foremost ones with fruit from the fruits of Paradise that they choose for themselves, which their souls desire, ﴿and the flesh of birds that they desire﴾. He says: they will also circulate among them with the flesh of birds, of whatever birds their souls desire.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 56, verse 22–26:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And [there will be] Houris, wide-eyed (22), like preserved pearls (23), as a reward for what they used to do (24). They will hear therein no ill speech nor sinning (25), except the saying "Peace, peace" (26).﴾

The reciters differed over the recitation of His words ﴿wa-ḥūrun ʿīn﴾. The majority of the reciters of Kufa and some of the people of Medina recited it ﴿wa-ḥūrin ʿīnin﴾ with the genitive (khafḍ), following the grammatical case of what precedes it, namely "fruit" and "meat," even though these are not the things one is served around (yuṭāfu bihi). But since its meaning is well known, the latter was made to follow the former in case, as some poets said:

"When the coquettish women appear one day, and they darken (zajjajna) the eyebrows and the eyes."

[This verse is one of the witnesses of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 323), and the discussion of it was previously given together with the witness "And you saw your husband in battle…" the two verses. In (al-Lisan: zajj) "the woman zajjat her eyebrow with the mazj: she made it fine and lengthened it. It was said: she lengthened it with antimony." And his words "When the coquettish women…" means only: "and they applied kohl to the eyes," as he said: "a drink of milk and dates and aqit cheese"

meaning: "and eating dates and aqit cheese," and there are many like it.

Another poet said: "I fed her straw…" i.e., "and I gave her cold water." He means that whatever comes of this kind comes by implying another verb with which the meaning is sound. Similar is the saying of another: "Would that your husband…" its estimate being: "and carrying a spear." Ibn Barri said: al-Jawhari mentioned the second half of a verse: "I made the woman's eyebrows zajj…" — "and they zajjin the eyebrows and the eyes." He said: it is by al-Ra'i and its correct form is "yuzajjijna." Its first half is: "And a shaking of an intoxication from a true tribe… they zajjijna the eyebrows and the eyes."

And after it: "Their camels kneeled at Dhat Ghasl… the chief of the day, they spread out the kudun."

Dhat Ghasl: a place. Yumahhidna: they make level. Al-Kudun: plural of kadan, which is what a woman lays under her mount, of cloth or the like.]

Thus "the eyes" are kohled, and only the eyebrows are shaped, so he returned it in case to "the eyebrows," for the hearer knows the meaning. And as another said:

"You hear from his innards a murmur, and for his two hands a stiffness and a spreading."

[This verse is one of the witnesses of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 323). In (al-Lisan: laghat) "al-laghat" (with the ghayn silent or vowelled) are confused sounds, varied, and noise that is not understood. In (al-Lisan: jasa’) "jasa'a al-shay' yajsa'u juswan" means it became hard and rough, and "jasa'at yaduhu min al-'amal" means it became stiff. The noun is al-jus'a, like al-jar'a. Al-jusa'a in animals is dryness of the joint, and a "jasi'a al-qawa'im" is an animal stiff in its legs. In (al-Lisan: badad): a horse "abad" is one with wide space between its forelegs, and it is said it is one whose forelegs are distant from its flanks, and this is the badad, and a camel "abda" is one with a twist in its forelegs. The point of the witness in the verse is that he conjoined "jusa'a" and "badad," and these are things seen, not heard, against "laghat," which is heard, and this is by an implied verb, i.e., "and you see for the two hands stiffness and spreading." It is thus like its counterparts among the witnesses al-Farra' mentions at this place. In the original (dal-dad) in place of (badad) is a distortion of the copyists.]

And al-jusa'a is a hardness in the hand, and it is not heard.

Some reciters of Medina, Mecca, Kufa and some of the people of Basra recited it in the nominative ﴿wa-ḥūrun ʿīn﴾ as an inceptive, and they said: the houris are not served around, so it is permissible to conjoin them in case to the case of fruit and meat; rather, it is nominative in the sense of: "and for them are houris, wide-eyed," or "they have houris, wide-eyed."

The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is to say: both are two well-known recitations, each of which has been recited by a group of reciters, with their meanings close, so whichever of the two recitations the reader recites is correct. "Ḥūr" is the plural of ḥawrāʾ, which is one whose eye is pure white and whose blackness is intense; and "ʿīn" is the plural of ʿaynāʾ, which is one large-eyed in beauty.

* *

And His words: ﴿like preserved pearls﴾

He says: they are in the purity of their whiteness and their beauty, like preserved pearls that are guarded in a case.

* *

And His words: ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾

He, exalted be His mention, says: a reward for them from God for their deeds which they used to do in the world, and a recompense for their obedience to Him.

The people of interpretation said what is similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr, from al-Hasan, regarding ﴿wa-ḥūrun ʿīn﴾: he said: intensely black: the blackness of the eye; intensely white: the whiteness of the eye.

- al-Hasan ibn 'Arafa narrated to us, he said: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Aslami narrated to us, from 'Abbad ibn Mansur al-Bajji, that he heard al-Hasan al-Basri say: al-ḥūr: the righteous women of the children of Adam.

- He said: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, who said: it reached me that the houris were created from saffron.

- al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-Tahhan narrated to us, he said: 'A'isha, the wife of Layth, narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: the houris were created from saffron.

- Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd al-Muharibi narrated to me, he said: 'Amr ibn Sa'd narrated to us, he said: I heard Layth tell me, from Mujahid, who said: the houris were created from saffron.

Others said: rather, the meaning of His words ﴿ḥūr﴾ is that the glance is bewildered by them.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Hisham narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid regarding ﴿wa-ḥūrun ʿīn﴾: he said: the glance is bewildered by them.

He said: "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that is in the shells, which no hand has touched."

And His words: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾

He says: they will not hear therein any speech except a saying of "peace": that is, safe from what they dislike.

As for the case of His words ﴿salāman salāman﴾, there are two possibilities: if you wish, you may make it follow "qīl," and "peace" will then itself be the "saying"; so it is as if it were said: "They will not hear therein ill speech nor sinning, except 'peace, peace'; but they will hear 'peace, peace.'" The second is that it be in the accusative by the action of "qīl" falling upon it, so its meaning would then be: "except the saying of 'peace.'" If one reads "salāman salāman" with tanwin, it is accusative by the action of "qīl" falling upon it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 56, verse 22–26:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And [there will be] Houris, wide-eyed (22), like preserved pearls (23), as a reward for what they used to do (24). They will hear therein no ill speech nor sinning (25), except the saying "Peace, peace" (26).﴾

The reciters differed over the recitation of His words ﴿wa-ḥūrun ʿīn﴾. The majority of the reciters of Kufa and some of the people of Medina recited it ﴿wa-ḥūrin ʿīnin﴾ with the genitive (khafḍ), following the grammatical case of what precedes it, namely "fruit" and "meat," even though these are not the things one is served around (yuṭāfu bihi). But since its meaning is well known, the latter was made to follow the former in case, as some poets said:

"When the coquettish women appear one day, and they darken (zajjajna) the eyebrows and the eyes."

[This verse is one of the witnesses of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 323), and the discussion of it was previously given together with the witness "And you saw your husband in battle…" the two verses. In (al-Lisan: zajj) "the woman zajjat her eyebrow with the mazj: she made it fine and lengthened it. It was said: she lengthened it with antimony." And his words "When the coquettish women…" means only: "and they applied kohl to the eyes," as he said: "a drink of milk and dates and aqit cheese"

meaning: "and eating dates and aqit cheese," and there are many like it.

Another poet said: "I fed her straw…" i.e., "and I gave her cold water." He means that whatever comes of this kind comes by implying another verb with which the meaning is sound. Similar is the saying of another: "Would that your husband…" its estimate being: "and carrying a spear." Ibn Barri said: al-Jawhari mentioned the second half of a verse: "I made the woman's eyebrows zajj…" — "and they zajjin the eyebrows and the eyes." He said: it is by al-Ra'i and its correct form is "yuzajjijna." Its first half is: "And a shaking of an intoxication from a true tribe… they zajjijna the eyebrows and the eyes."

And after it: "Their camels kneeled at Dhat Ghasl… the chief of the day, they spread out the kudun."

Dhat Ghasl: a place. Yumahhidna: they make level. Al-Kudun: plural of kadan, which is what a woman lays under her mount, of cloth or the like.]

Thus "the eyes" are kohled, and only the eyebrows are shaped, so he returned it in case to "the eyebrows," for the hearer knows the meaning. And as another said:

"You hear from his innards a murmur, and for his two hands a stiffness and a spreading."

[This verse is one of the witnesses of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 323). In (al-Lisan: laghat) "al-laghat" (with the ghayn silent or vowelled) are confused sounds, varied, and noise that is not understood. In (al-Lisan: jasa’) "jasa'a al-shay' yajsa'u juswan" means it became hard and rough, and "jasa'at yaduhu min al-'amal" means it became stiff. The noun is al-jus'a, like al-jar'a. Al-jusa'a in animals is dryness of the joint, and a "jasi'a al-qawa'im" is an animal stiff in its legs. In (al-Lisan: badad): a horse "abad" is one with wide space between its forelegs, and it is said it is one whose forelegs are distant from its flanks, and this is the badad, and a camel "abda" is one with a twist in its forelegs. The point of the witness in the verse is that he conjoined "jusa'a" and "badad," and these are things seen, not heard, against "laghat," which is heard, and this is by an implied verb, i.e., "and you see for the two hands stiffness and spreading." It is thus like its counterparts among the witnesses al-Farra' mentions at this place. In the original (dal-dad) in place of (badad) is a distortion of the copyists.]

And al-jusa'a is a hardness in the hand, and it is not heard.

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):** ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns,﴾ ﴿and acacias layered with fruit,﴾ ﴿and extended shade,﴾ ﴿and water poured forth.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾, who are those who will be taken on the Day of Resurrection to the right, those who were given their records in their right hands, O Muhammad. ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ What they are, what their state is, and what good has been prepared for them. It has also been said that they are the children of the believers.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, saying: Abu Hisham al-Makhzumi narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Qays narrated to us, that he heard Zadhan Abu Amr say: I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) say: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: "The companions of the right hand are the children of the believers."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: that is, what is their state, and what has been prepared for them. Then he began the report about what has been prepared for them in Paradise, and what their condition will be when they enter it, so He said: they are ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, meaning: among fruit of lote-trees laden with fruit, whose thorns have been removed.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil, those who engage in ta'wil, i.e., interpretation of the Qur'an) differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: what is meant by "khudud" (without thorns) is that which has been stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it.

Mention of those who said this:

• Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "He stripped it and made it heavy with fruit. It is said: it was stripped until its thorns disappeared, so there are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: Muhammad ibn Ikrimah claimed, saying: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdhah ibn Khalifah narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from Qassamah ibn Zuhayr, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "It was stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it."

• Abu Humayd al-Himsi Ahmad ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Amr ibn Abd Allah al-Ahmusi narrated to us, from al-Safr ibn Nusayr, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "Its thorns were stripped, so there are no thorns on it."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "We used to be told that it is the heavily laden one that has no thorns."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "It has no thorns."

• Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Ikrimah: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Humayd narrated this to me again, another time, from Mihran, with this chain, from Ikrimah, and he said: "It has no thorns, and it is laden with fruit."

Others said: rather, what is meant by it is that it is heavy with fruit.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿khudud (stripped)﴾, he said: "They say: this is the one heavy with fruit."

• Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "The heavily laden one."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "The heavily laden one."

His saying: ﴿and acacias layered with fruit﴾

* *

His saying: ﴿manḍūd (layered)﴾

That is, some of it is arranged upon others, and some of it is gathered together with other parts.

The interpreters have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd﴾: "Some of it upon others."

• al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd﴾: "Piled up, because they admire the shade of the (wajj) tree and its shadows, from its acacia and its lote-trees."

* *

His saying: ﴿and extended shade﴾

He says: they will be in a constant shade that the sun does not cancel out so as to destroy it. Everything that has no end is "mamdūd" (extended), as Labid said:

*"Time, long and enduring and extended, overcame survival, though I was not one to be overcome."*

[Footnote: The verse is by Labid. Abu Ubaydah attributed it to him in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 175b), and in his narration it reads "al-ghurrā'" instead of "al-baqā'" in the author's narration. The meaning: the long time overcame survival in this world, and nothing would overcome me except time. Abu Ubaydah recited it at the saying of Allah, "wa-ẓillin mamdūd," and said: "That is, the sun does not cancel it; it is constant. 'Mamdūd' is said of a long time or a life that does not end." Labid said: "Overcame survival..." (the verse).]

The traditions came with something similar to what we have said regarding this, and the scholars have held this view.

His saying: ﴿and water poured forth﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: and in it there is also flowing water, meaning poured out, flowing in no trench.

As:

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, regarding ﴿wa-māʾin maskūb﴾: "It flows in no trench."

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):** ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns,﴾ ﴿and acacias layered with fruit,﴾ ﴿and extended shade,﴾ ﴿and water poured forth.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾, who are those who will be taken on the Day of Resurrection to the right, those who were given their records in their right hands, O Muhammad. ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ What they are, what their state is, and what good has been prepared for them. It has also been said that they are the children of the believers.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, saying: Abu Hisham al-Makhzumi narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Qays narrated to us, that he heard Zadhan Abu Amr say: I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) say: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: "The companions of the right hand are the children of the believers."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: that is, what is their state, and what has been prepared for them. Then he began the report about what has been prepared for them in Paradise, and what their condition will be when they enter it, so He said: they are ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, meaning: among fruit of lote-trees laden with fruit, whose thorns have been removed.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil, those who engage in ta'wil, i.e., interpretation of the Qur'an) differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: what is meant by "khudud" (without thorns) is that which has been stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it.

It is said: it was stripped until its thorns disappeared, so there are no thorns on it."

• Abu Humayd al-Himsi Ahmad ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Amr ibn Abd Allah al-Ahmusi narrated to us, from al-Safr ibn Nusayr, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "Its thorns were stripped, so there are no thorns on it."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "We used to be told that it is the heavily laden one that has no thorns."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "It has no thorns."

His saying: ﴿manḍūd (layered)﴾

His saying: ﴿and extended shade﴾

He says: they will be in a constant shade that the sun does not cancel out so as to destroy it. Everything that has no end is "mamdūd" (extended), as Labid said:

*"Time, long and enduring and extended, overcame survival, though I was not one to be overcome."*

Abu Ubaydah recited it at the saying of Allah, "wa-ẓillin mamdūd," and said: "That is, the sun does not cancel it; it is constant. 'Mamdūd' is said of a long time or a life that does not end." Labid said: "Overcame survival..." (the verse).]

The traditions came with something similar to what we have said regarding this, and the scholars have held this view.

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):** ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns,﴾ ﴿and acacias layered with fruit,﴾ ﴿and extended shade,﴾ ﴿and water poured forth.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾, who are those who will be taken on the Day of Resurrection to the right, those who were given their records in their right hands, O Muhammad. ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ What they are, what their state is, and what good has been prepared for them. It has also been said that they are the children of the believers.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, saying: Abu Hisham al-Makhzumi narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Qays narrated to us, that he heard Zadhan Abu Amr say: I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) say: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: "The companions of the right hand are the children of the believers."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: that is, what is their state, and what has been prepared for them. Then he began the report about what has been prepared for them in Paradise, and what their condition will be when they enter it, so He said: they are ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, meaning: among fruit of lote-trees laden with fruit, whose thorns have been removed.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil, those who engage in ta'wil, i.e., interpretation of the Qur'an) differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: what is meant by "khudud" (without thorns) is that which has been stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it.

It is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to read ﴿wa-ṭalʿin manḍūd﴾ with the "ayn" (ʿ), i.e., "wa-ṭalʿin" meaning "banana clusters" (in place of "ṭalḥ," meaning acacia).

It is only ṭalʿ," and then he recited ﴿its spathe (ṭalʿuhā) is soft﴾. We said: "Shall we change it?" He said: "The Qur'an is not to be altered today, nor changed." As for ṭalḥ, al-Mu'ammar ibn al-Muthanna used to say: among the Arabs it is a large tree with many thorns, and he recited a verse of one of the camel-drivers (ḥudāh):

*"Her guide gave her good news and said: 'Tomorrow you will see the acacias and the sand-dunes.'"*

[Footnote: This is one of the verses cited by Abu Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 175, from the photographed copy of the manuscript "Murad Muntla" in Istanbul). He recited it at the saying of Allah, "wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd," and said: "The interpreters claim it is the banana; but the Arabs use ṭalḥ for a large tree with many thorns." The camel-driver said: "Her guide gave her good news..." (the two verses). As for "al-ḥibāl" with the ḥā' as in the narration of the author, it is the plural of ḥabl, which is a raised sand-dune that extends a long distance across the earth; with the jīm, as in Abu Ubaydah's narration, it is the plural of jabal (mountain). He gives the good news to his she-camel that she will reach her homeland tomorrow and see in it the acacia trees she is accustomed to, and the sand-dunes or mountains.]

* *

His saying: ﴿and water poured forth﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: and in it there is also flowing water, meaning poured out, flowing in no trench.

As:

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, regarding ﴿wa-māʾin maskūb﴾: "It flows in no trench."

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):** ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns,﴾ ﴿and acacias layered with fruit,﴾ ﴿and extended shade,﴾ ﴿and water poured forth.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾, who are those who will be taken on the Day of Resurrection to the right, those who were given their records in their right hands, O Muhammad. ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ What they are, what their state is, and what good has been prepared for them. It has also been said that they are the children of the believers.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us, saying: Abu Hisham al-Makhzumi narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Qays narrated to us, that he heard Zadhan Abu Amr say: I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) say: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: "The companions of the right hand are the children of the believers."

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ He said: that is, what is their state, and what has been prepared for them. Then he began the report about what has been prepared for them in Paradise, and what their condition will be when they enter it, so He said: they are ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, meaning: among fruit of lote-trees laden with fruit, whose thorns have been removed.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil, those who engage in ta'wil, i.e., interpretation of the Qur'an) differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: what is meant by "khudud" (without thorns) is that which has been stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it.

Mention of those who said this:

• Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "He stripped it and made it heavy with fruit. It is said: it was stripped until its thorns disappeared, so there are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: Muhammad ibn Ikrimah claimed, saying: "There are no thorns on it."

• Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdhah ibn Khalifah narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from Qassamah ibn Zuhayr, regarding His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "It was stripped of thorns, so there are no thorns on it."

• Abu Humayd al-Himsi Ahmad ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Amr ibn Abd Allah al-Ahmusi narrated to us, from al-Safr ibn Nusayr, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾, he said: "Its thorns were stripped, so there are no thorns on it."

His saying: ﴿and acacias layered with fruit﴾

As for al-Farra', he read it with the "ha'" (ḥ): ﴿wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd﴾, and it is thus in the codices of the people of the regions. It is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to read ﴿wa-ṭalʿin manḍūd﴾ with the "ayn" (ʿ), i.e., "wa-ṭalʿin" meaning "banana clusters" (in place of "ṭalḥ," meaning acacia).

• Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Zakariyya narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'd, from his father (may Allah be pleased with him), that he read it as ﴿wa-ṭalʿin manḍūd﴾.

• Sa'id ibn Yahya al-Umawi narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: Mujahid narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'd, from Qays ibn Sa'd, who said: A man recited ﴿wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd﴾ in the presence of Ali, and Ali said: "What is the matter with ṭalḥ? It is only ṭalʿ," and then he recited ﴿its spathe (ṭalʿuhā) is soft﴾. We said: "Shall we change it?" He said: "The Qur'an is not to be altered today, nor changed." As for ṭalḥ, al-Mu'ammar ibn al-Muthanna used to say: among the Arabs it is a large tree with many thorns, and he recited a verse of one of the camel-drivers (ḥudāh):

*"Her guide gave her good news and said: 'Tomorrow you will see the acacias and the sand-dunes.'"*

[Footnote: This is one of the verses cited by Abu Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 175, from the photographed copy of the manuscript "Murad Muntla" in Istanbul). He recited it at the saying of Allah, "wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd," and said: "The interpreters claim it is the banana; but the Arabs use ṭalḥ for a large tree with many thorns." The camel-driver said: "Her guide gave her good news..." (the two verses). As for "al-ḥibāl" with the ḥā' as in the narration of the author, it is the plural of ḥabl, which is a raised sand-dune that extends a long distance across the earth; with the jīm, as in Abu Ubaydah's narration, it is the plural of jabal (mountain). He gives the good news to his she-camel that she will reach her homeland tomorrow and see in it the acacia trees she is accustomed to, and the sand-dunes or mountains.]

His saying: ﴿manḍūd (layered)﴾

That is, some of it is arranged upon others, and some of it is gathered together with other parts.

The interpreters have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd﴾: "Some of it upon others."

His saying: ﴿and extended shade﴾

He says: they will be in a constant shade that the sun does not cancel out so as to destroy it. Everything that has no end is "mamdūd" (extended), as Labid said:

*"Time, long and enduring and extended, overcame survival, though I was not one to be overcome."*

[Footnote: The verse is by Labid. Abu Ubaydah attributed it to him in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 175b), and in his narration it reads "al-ghurrā'" instead of "al-baqā'" in the author's narration. The meaning: the long time overcame survival in this world, and nothing would overcome me except time. Abu Ubaydah recited it at the saying of Allah, "wa-ẓillin mamdūd," and said: "That is, the sun does not cancel it; it is constant. 'Mamdūd' is said of a long time or a life that does not end." Labid said: "Overcame survival..." (the verse).]

The traditions came with something similar to what we have said regarding this, and the scholars have held this view.
